citation: "Early Chicago Streets." Chicagology. Transcribing A. T. Andreas, History of Chicago, Volume I (1884), including its block quotation from "Brass's History".
locator: Section headed "History of Chicago, Volume I, A. T. Andreas, 1884": paragraphs 1-2 for the 1833-36 street orders, and the indented block quotation from Brass's History beginning "I said we had no pavements in 1848".
note:
THE 1830s STREET ORDERS, verbatim: "In August the town of Chicago was incorporated, and one of the orders of the Trustees was given to the first official orders of the Trustees was given to the Surveyor to 'pitch' South Water Street from the United States Reservation to Randolph Street, on or before April, 1834." (the doubled clause is the page's OCR damage, and it recurs identically on chicagology_southwaterstreet). Then: "During July, 1834, the Surveyor was required to graduate South Water Street, so that 'water should flow from each cross street into the river.' South Water and Lake streets were the two principal thoroughfares of the village, and therefore were early turnpiked and graded. Plank sluices were also built across Clark Street, to carry the drainage to the South Branch, and that street was somewhat improved in 1836." And: "By the winter of 1836 the leading thoroughfares were turnpiked." The statute-labour regime is here too: Benjamin Jones street commissioner, the law empowering him "to call out anybody between the ages of twenty-one and sixty years, to work upon the streets and bridges for three days per annum" within a mile of the town limits.

THE DATE TRAP, AND IT HAS ALREADY REACHED A DOSSIER. docs/research/01-terrain-hydrology.md line 78 cites this page for "Streets 'impassable' for weeks each spring; empty wagons and drays mired on Lake and Water Streets" without a date. On the page, that sentence is inside a block quotation from Brass's History which OPENS: "I said we had no pavements in 1848. The streets were simply thrown up as country roads. In the spring for weeks, portions of them would be impassable. I have at different times seen empty wagons and drays stuck on Lake and Water streets on even block between Wabash Avenue and the river." That is 1848 Chicago - THIRTEEN YEARS after the scene date, a city of twenty thousand rather than a town of three, with Wabash Avenue built out. Everything else in the same quotation is later still: the joke signboards, the digging-down and planking of Lake Street, and "the Common Council established a grade from two to six or eight feet above the natural level of the soil", which the page immediately dates by adding that the planking of Lake Street "was ordered by the Common Council January 22, 1849". docs/research/01-terrain-hydrology.md line 47 does hedge that grade with "eventually"; line 78 does not hedge the mud. Neither sentence may drive an 1835 street surface.

WHAT THIS PAGE DOES NOT CONTAIN AT ALL: the stage and the mail. The brief for this record described it as "the stage and mail service, wagons and drays mired on Lake and Water Streets". The word "mail" occurs on the page twice, both times in the comment form's "Email" field; "stage" does not occur. Its 1833 opening is about the State road to Vincennes and "various minor roads", not about coaching. Anything about the stage or the mail must come from elsewhere - see chicagology_first_post_office for the post office, and note that chicagology_prefire021 has the one stage sentence reached so far, about the stage being unable to reach the Tremont corner in spring.

THE FROG POND IS NOT A THIRD WITNESS. "As late as July 9, 1836, the American calls attention to a pond of water on Lake Street, corner of La Salle, inhabited by frogs." is the same Andreas sentence already recorded at chicagology_prefire062 and reprinted again on chicagology_southwaterstreet. One sentence, three pages.
